content: Aromatase inhibitors have been studied as a potential treatment to improve height outcomes in male children and adolescents with short stature. This is based on their ability to inhibit the conversion of testosterone to oestradiol, which plays a critical role in the closure of growth plates (epiphyseal closure). By delaying this process, the treatment aims to extend the period of growth. The primary objective of this research was to evaluate the effects of aromatase inhibitors on height outcomes in male children and adolescents with short stature. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the WHO ICTRP trial register, covering studies up to August 2014. Additional citation searches and reference list screenings were performed to ensure all relevant trials were included. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the use of aromatase inhibitors with placebo in this population. Two independent reviewers screened the studies for relevance, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework, and study authors were contacted for missing information. The primary outcomes assessed were final or near-final height, adverse events, and health-related quality of life. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, cognitive outcomes, socioeconomic effects, laboratory measures, short-term growth parameters, and bone health. Due to significant clinical heterogeneity among the trials, a meta-analysis was not feasible, and the findings were presented narratively. Four RCTs involving 207 participants were included in the review. Of these, 84 participants received aromatase inhibitors. The trials included male participants with conditions such as constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), idiopathic short stature (ISS), and growth hormone (GH) deficiency. Three of the trials demonstrated a low or unclear risk of bias for the primary outcomes. All trials reported improvements in short-term growth outcomes, such as predicted adult height. However, only one trial provided data on final or near-final height, and this was reported under non-randomized conditions. None of the trials assessed health-related quality of life. Adverse events were reported in one publication. Notably, 45% of prepubertal boys with ISS who were treated with letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, developed mild morphological abnormalities in their vertebrae. In contrast, no such abnormalities were observed in the placebo group. In conclusion, the available evidence suggests that aromatase inhibitors can improve short-term growth outcomes in male children and adolescents with short stature. However, there is no robust evidence to support an increase in final adult height, as only one of the four trials reported final height data, and this was under non-randomized conditions. Further research is needed to clarify the long-term effects and safety of this intervention.
